extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (aesthetics) interested in Kantian theory of taste
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Kant's criteria for aesthetic (judgements of taste) evaluation: distinctions between pure/empirical judgements, the role of purposiveness, the exclusion of interest/emotion, the free vs dependent beauty distinction, and the status of universal assent (sensus communis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pure judgement of taste
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgement of taste on which charm and emotion have no influence — which therefore has as its determining ground merely the purposiveness of the form — is a pure judgement of taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pure judgements are contemplative, not practical; their determining ground is the formal purposiveness of the representation in the subject, not any empirical pleasure, interest, or concept. Anti-pattern: treating charm or emotion as the grounds for calling something beautiful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: empirical (material) vs pure (formal) aesthetical judgements
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetical judgements can be divided into empirical (the first assert pleasantness or unpleasantness; judgements of Sense, material aesthetical judgements) and pure (the second assert the beauty of an object or manner of representing it; formal judgements of Taste).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical judgements evaluate pleasantness (sensations); pure judgements evaluate form and claim beauty. When producing or assessing an aesthetic judgement, identify whether the ground is sensation (material) or form (formal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity of sensation as condition for colour/tone beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensations of colours and of tone have a right to be regarded as beautiful only insofar as they are pure; this determination concerns their form and admits of universal communicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple, 'pure' colours/tones may be judged beautiful because their form admits communicability; composite colours lack a standard for purity. Example: single colour or tone may be regarded as beautiful only if free from distracting foreign sensations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charm and emotion spoil impartiality of taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Every interest spoils the judgement of taste and takes from its impartiality, especially if the purposiveness is grounded on the feeling of pleasure rather than preceding it (interest of Reason).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgements that rest on charm or emotion cannot claim universally valid satisfaction; calling charm or emotion the measure of assent is 'barbaric'. Anti-pattern: substituting matter of satisfaction (charm) for form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form (delineation/composition) over charm in formative arts
rubrics_metrics.description: In painting, sculpture, and all formative arts (architecture, horticulture) the delineation (or composition in time) is the essential thing; colours/tones belong to charm and cannot make something worthy of contemplation or beautiful unless they serve the form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate formative works primarily on how form/delineation/composition render the object intelligible as a whole; colours and ornaments may enliven but should not be allowed to substitute for formal beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornament versus finery
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornaments (parerga) augment the satisfaction of taste only by their form; if an ornament does not consist in beautiful form and is used merely to recommend the painting by its charm, it is finery and injures genuine beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish legitimate ornament (formal complement that integrates with the object) from mere finery (decorative charm that distracts). Examples: picture frames/draperies legitimate only if formally consonant; golden frames used solely for recommendation are finery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotion does not belong to beauty; sublimity requires separate standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotion (a sensation in which pleasantness is produced by a momentary checking and consequent outflow of vital force) does not belong at all to beauty; sublimity — with which emotion is bound up — requires a different standard of judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate emotional arousal or excitement with beauty; treat the sublime by its own criteria rather than as an aesthetical judgement of beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty independent of concept of perfection (Good)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Beautiful (judged on formal purposiveness) is quite independent of the concept of the Good (objective purposiveness, i.e., utility or internal perfection); beauty cannot be resolved into perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid evaluating beauty by reference to objective purposes (utility or perfection). Anti-pattern: reducing beauty to usefulness or to degree of perfection as a concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective purposiveness versus objective purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: The formal element in representation gives a subjective purposiveness of the subject's cognitive state (a facility of apprehending form) but furnishes no objective purposiveness or perfection of the object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging beauty, recognize that the 'purposiveness' is a feature of the play of cognitive faculties, not a property that implies the object serves an external or internal purpose (contrasted with utility or perfection). Example: a circular clearing in a forest evokes purposiveness without implying a function.

rubrics_metrics.name: No objective rule of taste via concepts; feeling is determining ground
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be no objective rule of taste which shall determine by means of concepts what is beautiful; the aesthetical judgement's determining ground is the feeling (of internal sense), not a concept of the object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not seek to ground judgements of taste on conceptual rules; instead, acknowledge their basis in subjective feeling while aiming for communicability. This undergirds the claim that aesthetic necessity is 'exemplary' rather than apodictic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free beauty (pulchritudo vaga) versus dependent/adherent beauty (pulchritudo adhaerens)
rubrics_metrics.description: Free beauty presupposes no concept of what the object ought to be; dependent beauty presupposes such a concept and the perfection of the object in accordance with it. Free beauty is the basis of pure judgements of taste; dependent (adherent) beauty is tied to purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify examples accordingly: flowers, abstract patterns, wordless music as free beauty; human beauty, animal breed beauty, buildings as dependent beauty. When beauty is dependent, the judgement is not purely aesthetic and may be subject to rules tied to purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity of judgement lost when conditioned by concept of purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgement of taste which declares an object beautiful under the condition of a definite concept (purpose) is not pure; when beauty is judged in reference to internal purpose, satisfaction is grounded on a concept and not purely form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the evaluator applies a concept of 'what the object ought to be' (e.g., a church must be suitable for worship) the judgement pertains to design/unification with reason, not to pure taste. Such rules are rules for unifying taste with reason, not rules of taste per se.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal Idea versus Ideal of beauty (human case)
rubrics_metrics.description: Normal Idea: an individual intuition serving as a standard for the race (an average produced by the imagination). Ideal: for human beauty, includes expression of the moral — the visible expression of moral Ideas makes possible a higher Ideal of beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish the average/correctness standard (normal Idea) used for species-wide judgement from the Ideal that integrates moral expression (unique to humanity). The normal Idea yields correctness without positive universal pleasing; the Ideal aims at positive universal approval by including moral content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty defined as form of purposiveness without representation of purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty is the form of the purposiveness of an object, so far as this is perceived in it without any representation of a purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This concise definition is the theoretical core: when perceiving beauty, we perceive purposiveness of form but do not represent any purpose for the object. Use this as a test: can the object's purposiveness be felt without positing a purpose?

rubrics_metrics.name: Modal claim: necessity of aesthetic judgement is 'exemplary' not apodictic
rubrics_metrics.description: The beautiful we think as having a necessary reference to satisfaction; this necessity is peculiar: not theoretical (apodictic) nor practical, but exemplary — a necessity of the assent of all to a judgement regarded as an example of a universal rule that cannot be stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making strong claims about universal approval, recognize the special status: one claims 'ought' (everyone ought to agree) but without grounding in concepts; the necessity is subjective-exemplary and distinct from logical proof or moral obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of agreement; the 'ought' of taste is conditioned
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgement of taste requires the agreement of every one; the speaker who describes something as beautiful claims that every one ought to give approval — this 'ought' is pronounced in accordance with all required data for judging and yet is only conditioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims of universal assent are conditional on correct subsumption under the relevant (subjective) ground; evaluators should be aware that appeals to universal assent depend on shared cognitive grounds, not on objective proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presupposition of a common sense (sensus communis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity which is thought in an aesthetical judgement presupposes a common sense — not common understanding by concepts but a common feeling-ground arising from the free play of cognitive powers — as the subjective principle that enables universal communicability of aesthetic feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To justify claims of universal communicability, assume a shared 'sensus communis' that makes feelings communicable. This is an ideal norm (not empirical) that grounds the 'exemplary' force of taste judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground for presupposing common sense: universal communicability of cognition and feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: We have grounds for assuming a common sense because cognitions and the accompanying state of mind must admit universal communicability for harmony between them and the Object; the universal communicability of feeling presupposes a common sense as necessary condition of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as justificatory backing when claiming that an aesthetic judgement seeks universal communicability; the assumption is methodological rather than empirical, invoked to avoid scepticism about shared judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective necessity represented as objective via the common sense ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity of universal agreement in a judgement of taste is subjective but is represented as objective under the presupposition of a common sense; common sense acts as an ideal norm permitting one to claim that others 'ought' to agree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting the universal validity of an aesthetic judgement, be explicit that this objectivity is a projected ideal based on the presupposed common sense. Treat disagreements as possible mis-subsumptions rather than outright refutations of the ideal.
